findings.title: Django ORM raises AssertionError on negative slice indices
findings.body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset set to a negative value. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts that slice indices are non-negative and raises `AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported.')` when they are not. The in-line comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', which is false. Any superuser or global admin who sends a cursor URL parameter like `cursor=0:-1:0` to the audit logs endpoint (which unconditionally sets enable_advanced_features=True for those users) will cause an unhandled AssertionError, producing a 500 response.

findings.title: Negative offset still crashes BasePaginator for is_prev=True
findings.body: The BasePaginator.get_result change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` only clamps negative offsets for the non-prev branch. When cursor.is_prev is True and cursor.offset is negative, start_offset stays negative and the subsequent `queryset[start_offset:stop]` triggers Django's 'Negative indexing is not supported' AssertionError. The accompanying comment ('This is safe because the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions') is incorrect; Django explicitly disallows negative slice indices on querysets.

findings.title: Endpoint unconditionally enables broken advanced pagination path
findings.body: When the user is a superuser or has global access, the endpoint passes `enable_advanced_features=True` to OptimizedCursorPaginator. Combined with the fact that `Cursor.__str__`/`from_string` round-trip a user-supplied integer offset verbatim, any such user can craft a cursor with a negative value (e.g. `?cursor=0:-1:0`) to crash the endpoint with AssertionError. There is no validation, no length/offset bound check, and no fallback; the new paginator code path is a denial-of-service for the most privileged users. The gating mechanism is also confused: `optimized_pagination=true` from the request is checked but plays no role, while the actual crash vector (cursor.offset) is unvalidated.

findings.title: Silent per-span data loss replaces whole-segment drop
findings.body: When the post-union ZSET cardinality exceeds 1000, the script executes `zpopmin` to drop the oldest (lowest end_timestamp_precise) members. This is a fundamental semantic change from the previous consumer-side check in buffer.py (which dropped the entire segment via `del payloads[key]`) to silently dropping individual members during insertion. For traces where the root span arrives late, child spans already buffered can be evicted before the root arrives, producing incomplete segments that are still flushed downstream with no error. There is no metric for evicted spans, no test coverage, and the eviction strategy (lowest end_timestamp_precise) is not justified.

findings.title: Redirect chain depth limit silently lowered 10x
findings.body: The redirect-resolution loop cap was reduced from 10000 to 1000, removing the previous safety comment about depth 10k. The PR description provides no rationale for this change. Any trace whose segment tree has a redirect chain between 1001 and 10000 deep will now exit the loop before resolving to the final set_span_id, leaving the new span attached to a stale set and producing a split/broken segment instead of one correctly-merged segment. This change affects production correctness for deeply nested traces and is not covered by tests.

findings.title: KeyError if end_timestamp_precise is missing from event
findings.body: The factory reads `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` with direct subscript access. Unlike `parent_span_id`, which is read via `val.get(...)`, this field is treated as required. The SpanEvent schema may evolve or upstream producers (older relays, batched ingest) may omit it; any such event will raise KeyError inside the consumer, killing the batch and potentially stalling the partition. The newly added test only covers the happy path where the field is present.

findings.title: ZUNIONSTORE default SUM aggregation distorts end_timestamp_precise scores
findings.body: Both unions use the default `AGGREGATE SUM` semantics: when the same member is present in both the destination set_key and the incoming source (parent_key on the second union, span_key on the first if a previous batch had landed it there), the resulting score becomes `original_score + new_score` instead of staying at `end_timestamp_precise`. This makes scores meaningless sums of microsecond-precision timestamps, which silently changes the ordering produced by `zscan` and biases `zpopmin` eviction (summed members get higher scores, making them less likely to be evicted). It is also undocumented and not tested.

findings.title: max_segment_spans parameter no longer enforced
findings.body: SpansBuffer still accepts `max_segment_spans: int = 1001` in __init__ but the consumer-side enforcement that used this limit in _load_segment_data was deleted without removing the parameter. The limit is now controlled entirely by the hardcoded 1000 in add-buffer.lua. Any caller that tuned max_segment_spans is silently overridden by a magic number in the Lua script; the parameter is dead config.

findings.title: zscan on legacy SET keys will raise WRONGTYPE during deploys
findings.body: The consumer now issues `p.zscan(key, ...)` against every segment key, but the on-disk format previously used Redis SETs. On rolling deploys where new consumer instances coexist with old data, or after a partial rollback, zscan against a SET key returns `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`. There is no version/key-type check, no migration step, and no metric for this condition, so segments will silently fail to load and the consumer will lose data for the affected trace until the keys TTL out.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates Paginator almost verbatim
findings.body: The new OptimizedCursorPaginator re-implements get_item_key and value_from_cursor exactly as Paginator does (Paginator already inherits these from BasePaginator), and re-implements get_result as a near-copy of BasePaginator.get_result. The only meaningful difference is the `enable_advanced_features` branch that itself crashes. This is dead code masquerading as a feature; it is brittle (any future change to BasePaginator.get_result will need to be mirrored) and the misleading docstring advertises capabilities (negative offsets) that don't actually work.

findings.title: Cursor accepts arbitrary int offset with no validation
findings.body: Cursor.__init__ now advertises 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' but accepts any integer without bound or sign validation. Combined with the broken negative-offset handling downstream, this lets any caller of Cursor.from_string feed extreme or malicious values (e.g. -2**31) into the paginator. Even with negative-offset slicing eventually corrected upstream, an attacker can still trigger expensive queries via large positive offsets (which are also unbounded).

findings.title: No tests cover the new >1000-span eviction behavior
findings.body: The Lua script's `zpopmin`-based eviction when span_count > 1000 is a new behavioral guarantee with data-integrity implications, but no test inserts more than a handful of spans per segment. There is no test for: (a) which spans get evicted (oldest by end_timestamp_precise?); (b) that the eviction actually caps cardinality at 1000; (c) that segments exceeding 1000 spans still flush correctly and don't get dropped; (d) that the metric/observability for evictions exists. The PR therefore lacks coverage of its headline feature.

findings.title: Test payloads omit end_timestamp_precise validation
findings.body: Existing tests were retrofitted to add `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0`, but the only new test value is a constant used uniformly. There is no test asserting that missing end_timestamp_precise produces a clear error (vs. the KeyError that the current code raises), no test for non-finite or negative values, and no test verifying that two spans with the same end_timestamp_precise are still both retained (zadd behavior on score collision is not asserted).

findings.title: Comments describe a feature that does not exist
findings.body: The added inline comments describe 'Performance optimization for high-volume audit log access patterns', 'optimized paginator for high-performance audit log navigation', and 'enhanced cursor support' — but the OptimizedCursorPaginator it routes to is a copy of Paginator with a feature (negative offsets) that crashes Django. The `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter is checked but does not influence which features are actually exposed. The comments mislead future maintainers about what the code does and why.

findings.title: Comments falsely claim queryset handles negative slicing
findings.body: Both the BasePaginator change at line ~179 and the OptimizedCursorPaginator comment at line ~876 assert 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions' / 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. This is incorrect: Django raises AssertionError on negative slice indices. Comments that document safety properties that are not true make future debugging harder and may cause contributors to rely on a guarantee that does not exist.
